column4: The section sets a vizr down; here war itself “lays down its burdens” (تَضَعَ الْحَرْبُ أَوْزَارَهَا), joining both named roots in one concrete idiom and showing that awzār can be the weight and equipment of conflict rather than personal sin.

The unlettered messenger “lays down from them their burden and the shackles” (يَضَعُ عَنْهُمْ إِصْرَهُمْ وَالْأَغْلَالَ), repeating the section’s verb, preposition, removal from a person, and secondary fetter image while making the relieved addressee a reliever of others.

Those surprised by the Hour carry “their burdens upon their backs” (أَوْزَارَهُمْ عَلَىٰ ظُهُورِهِمْ); vizr and zahr form the section’s exact bodily scene, but the load remains instead of being taken off.

“No bearer bears another’s burden,” and even a heavily laden soul that calls for help has none of it carried; this gives the rule against transferred liability that makes the section’s divine removal exceptional without making God another accountable bearer.
The one who turns away from the Reminder carries a vizr on Resurrection Day; it directly reverses the section’s movement in which the vizr is removed and dhikr is raised.
Following 20:100’s bearer, this ayah calls the carried thing an evil load (حِمْلًا), supplying the felt weight of the vizr that refusal of remembrance leaves in place.
Misleaders carry their own awzār in full and some of the burdens of those they mislead; the ayah distinguishes personal guilt from the added liability caused by making others stray.

After the empty offer in 29:12, the misleaders really do carry their own weights and further weights with them; the addition is causal liability, not the innocent transfer forbidden by the section’s burden rule.
The unbelievers say, “Follow our way, and we will carry your errors”; this voiced offer stages precisely the impossible substitute bearer that 29:13 and the section’s cited rule correct.

The calf-makers say they were made to carry awzār from the people’s ornaments; these are portable goods, giving the Qur’anic concrete baseline for the section’s cloth bundle before vizr becomes moral weight.

The Prophet is told to ask whether he should seek a lord other than God when every soul earns against itself and no bearer bears another’s vizr; this directly states the individual-accountability boundary behind the removed load.
Guidance and straying accrue to the person, and “no bearer bears another’s burden”; this occurrence grounds the burden rule in each person’s response to guidance.
Within the contrast between disbelief and gratitude, the ayah says no bearer bears another’s vizr; it ties the image’s weight to one’s own stance toward God rather than transferable cargo.
The scrolls of Moses and Abraham contain the rule that no bearer bears another’s vizr, locating the section’s burden boundary in an older revealed teaching.

The prayer asks, “Do not load upon us a burden” (لَا تَحْمِلْ عَلَيْنَا إِصْرًا), while the ayah first says no soul is charged beyond capacity; it turns the section’s relieved weight into a communal plea to the same Lord.
“God desires to lighten from you” because the human was created weak; this states directly what the section makes audible through a back strained until its load is removed.
A mother carries her child in hardship and puts it down in hardship (حَمَلَتْهُ ... وَوَضَعَتْهُ), a bodily instance in which carrying ends through the section’s named act of setting down.
At the Hour every pregnant one “puts down her load” (تَضَعُ كُلُّ ذَاتِ حَمْلٍ حَمْلَهَا); the same bodily verb-object relation makes the release sudden and overwhelming.
For pregnant women the term lasts until “they put down their load” (يَضَعْنَ حَمْلَهُنَّ), an ordinary embodied counterpart to a weight being taken from its bearer.
The command to maintain pregnant women until they put down their load repeats the concrete carrying-and-release scene while attaching duties of care to it.
Livestock carry people’s heavy loads to a land they could reach only with great bodily strain; the scene makes the hardship of bearing weight visible without moralizing the cargo.
A mother carries her child “in weakness upon weakness”; the cumulative bodily strain corresponds to the section’s weight known through what it does to the bearer.

The heavens, earth, and mountains refuse the Trust, while the human carries it; this is the Qur’an’s largest contrast between an entrusted weight that must be borne and the unnamed weight that is removed.
The donkey carrying books stages a back loaded with revelation that the bearer does not comprehend; it sharply separates physically bearing scripture from the raised, living dhikr in the section.
The “carrier of firewood” turns carrying into a person’s defining posture and punishment, an adverse bodily counterpart to the addressee whose load has been removed.
The rope of palm fibre around the carrier’s neck completes 111:4’s load scene and closely meets the section’s secondary image of a cord joined to restraint.
God “raised” the sky and “set” the balance (رَفَعَهَا وَوَضَعَ الْمِيزَانَ); the two named roots appear together, making the section’s load-down/name-up movement part of an ordered vertical pair.
God permits houses “to be raised” and His name to be remembered in them; elevation and dhikr meet in one ayah, closely paralleling the raising of the addressee’s remembrance.

Good speech ascends to God and righteous action raises it; verbal remembrance acquires upward movement, clarifying that the section’s raised “name” is honor and accepted speech rather than a lifted object.
God grants Abraham and his family “a lofty tongue of truth,” an enduring honorable reputation that directly parallels a remembrance raised for the prophetic addressee.
Abraham asks for “a tongue of truth among later people”; the prayer names the lasting good mention that the section describes spatially as raised dhikr.
The Qur’an is “a dhikr for you and your people,” addressing the Prophet with the same word that the section says God raised for him and locating that honor in revelation.
Moses asks, “My Lord, expand for me my breast” (اشْرَحْ لِي صَدْرِي); it is the clearest other prophetic plea for the bodily opening recalled at the front of this section.
Moses next asks God to ease his task; the ayah states as a request what the section’s taken-off load makes perceptible in the Prophet’s mission.

The one whose breast God expands for submission stands in divine light, while the ayah ends with hard hearts; it gives the opened front of the body a spiritual consequence that complements the relieved back.
God charges a soul only according to what He has given it and “will make after hardship ease”; capacity, load, and the surah’s ensuing promise of ease converge in one rule.
“We shall ease you toward ease” is a divine plural promise to the Prophet, stating directly the ease embodied by taking a back-straining burden from him.

Shackles rise to the unbelievers’ chins so their heads are forced up; this literal restraint closely realizes the section’s dictionary image of a bound person holding up the cord of his fetter, while distinguishing forced elevation from raised honor.
Each person’s fate is fastened to his neck and a record is brought out for him; personal accountability is attached to the body as concretely as the section’s burden rests on the back.
The person given his record from behind his back embodies guilt at the rear of the body and proceeds toward ruin, reversing the addressee whose back has already been relieved.
The sick or rain-struck fighters may “put down your weapons” (تَضَعُوا أَسْلِحَتَكُمْ); the named verb denotes literal relief from carried equipment while the command preserves necessary caution.
The section’s dictionary definition glosses setting down with ḥaṭṭ; the commanded word حِطَّةٌ is followed by forgiveness, joining the physical language of lowering to remission of faults.
The repeated command to say حِطَّةٌ at the gate again makes “lowering/remission” the spoken route to sins being forgiven, matching the section’s movement from weight to guilt and release.

The same divine “We” promises to cast upon the Prophet “a heavy word” (قَوْلًا ثَقِيلًا); it marks the boundary between a disabling burden removed from him and the weighty revelation he is still entrusted to receive.
“We did not send down the Qur’an upon you that you should suffer”; descent “upon” the Prophet does not make revelation the harmful weight the section says was taken “from” him.

God expands the breast of the one guided, but makes the breast of one led astray tight and constricted as though climbing into the sky; the same bodily site displays both relief and crushing resistance.
God knows the Prophet’s breast is constricted by what opponents say; this remembered pressure gives a concrete contrary state to the expanded front and relieved back.

The Prophet is warned that his breast may be constricted by demands and rejection of revelation; the ayah supplies a specific pressure of mission without claiming that it exhausts the section’s deliberately unnamed vizr.

A person who “opens his breast to disbelief” uses bodily expansion for willing unbelief, setting a moral boundary around the section’s gracious expansion and preventing openness itself from being treated as automatically good.
God could have raised the man by His signs, but he clings to the earth and follows desire; upward exaltation is refused for downward attachment, clarifying the moral force of a raised name.
The Event is “abasing, raising” (خَافِضَةٌ رَّافِعَةٌ); its paired reversals show that elevation may be judgment and rank, not merely the mechanical opposite of setting down a load.
Believers must not raise their voices above the Prophet’s voice; human vocal elevation over him is forbidden even as God raises his remembrance, distinguishing honor from loudness.
The Prophet’s hater is the one cut off; that loss of posterity and mention supplies the personal reverse of the enduring remembrance raised for the addressee.
God raises the Mount above Israel while commanding them to hold revelation firmly; a massive weight is suspended over the addressees rather than removed from them.
The repeated raising of the Mount above Israel accompanies a covenant they answer with disobedience; it contrasts an overhead coercive mass with the section’s relieved body and raised honor.
The Mount is raised above the People of the Book for their covenant, making elevation threatening when the lifted object is a mountain over human bodies rather than a name for someone.
The mountain is torn up above the people like a canopy and they think it will fall upon them; this is the section’s load relation reversed into an enormous weight poised overhead.
A group casts God’s Book “behind their backs”; instead of God taking a burden off the back and raising dhikr, people themselves put revelation behind the back and reject it.
Those charged to explain scripture cast it behind their backs for a small price; the back becomes the place where remembrance is discarded, clarifying the moral opposite of raised remembrance.
Shuʿayb tells his people they have taken God “behind your backs” as something disregarded; it uses the rear of the body for neglect rather than for a load mercifully removed.
The hand must be neither shackled to the neck nor spread to its furthest reach; this bodily restraint gives the section’s fetter image an ethical boundary between paralysis and ruinous release.
“Freeing a neck” is the direct humane reversal of the section’s cord, shackle, and burden imagery: restraint is physically undone at the body that bears it.
The cry “no refuge” uses وَزَر in the sense of shelter, not the section’s وِزْر as load; the vocalized lexical boundary matters because the same consonants otherwise invite a false burden reading.

The woman who undoes her spun yarn after strength uses the named n-q-ḍ root for physical unravelling; this differs from the section’s branch in which the same root makes a weighted joint audibly creak rather than saying it broke.
“Do not break the oaths” uses n-q-ḍ for violating a binding commitment; the contrast guards the section’s أَنقَضَ from being flattened into moral breach instead of audible bodily strain.
Those of understanding do not break the covenant (لَا يَنقُضُونَ الْمِيثَاقَ); this negative covenant sense contrasts with the section’s specialized sound of a burdened back.
Those who break God’s covenant use n-q-ḍ in the transgressive covenant sense; the shared root but different action helps preserve the creaking, not covenant-breaking, of the section’s back.
The losers “break God’s covenant” after its confirmation; this recurrent Qur’anic n-q-ḍ sense provides a lexical boundary for the rarer joint-sound sense developed in the section.
Israel’s breaking of its covenant again uses n-q-ḍ for violation, not the audible result of weight; the distinction prevents the back in the section from being said to have been broken.
Because they broke their covenant, hearts are hardened; the moral rupture belongs to this ayah’s context and contrasts with the section’s bodily creak under load.
People who repeatedly break their treaty use n-q-ḍ for recurring betrayal; that agency and moral object differ from a load causing a passive back to sound.
The miser who denies the best is “eased toward hardship”; the paradox reverses the section’s relief and shows that being facilitated can lead toward a difficult end rather than release.
God leaves Noah a remembrance among later generations; this lasting presence after him is a concrete nonlexical parallel to having one’s dhikr raised.
“Peace upon Noah among the worlds” supplies the honored words preserved by 37:78’s remembrance, showing what an elevated name sounds like in later mouths.
God leaves Abraham a remembrance among later generations, fulfilling the prayer for lasting truthful mention and paralleling the section’s raised dhikr.
“Peace upon Abraham” gives the content of 37:108’s surviving remembrance and thus an enacted example of an honored prophetic name.
God leaves Moses and Aaron a remembrance among later generations; the plural pair shows that enduring honor can attach to co-workers in a burdened mission.
“Peace upon Moses and Aaron” voices the memorial preserved in 37:119, making raised remembrance audible rather than spatial.
God leaves Elijah a remembrance among later generations, repeating the pattern in which divine speech sustains a prophet’s honorable name.
“Peace upon Ilyāsīn” states the remembered greeting promised by 37:129 and gives another concrete form of elevated mention.

God says He sent down a Book “in which is your dhikr”; whether read as reminder or honor, it locates the audience’s standing in revelation and provides a communal analogue to the Prophet’s raised dhikr.
God raises some messengers in degrees above others; the same root moves from physical lifting to prophetic rank, the semantic move required when the section raises a name.
God raises Idris to a high station; personal exaltation rather than cargo-lifting helps define the honor sense of the section’s fourth-ayah verb.
God raises believers and people of knowledge in degrees; this shared root explicitly means granted rank, supporting the reading of raised remembrance as bestowed honor.
Paradise contains couches “raised high”; beside the cups set down in 88:14, the physical arrangement instantiates the section’s lexical up/down pair, though on separate objects.
Cups are “set out” (مَوْضُوعَةٌ) beside the raised couches of 88:13; the juxtaposition concretizes وضع against رفع without implying that the cups are burdens.
After 55:7 raises the sky and sets the balance, God “lays out” the earth for creatures; it extends the vertical ordering of the same وضع root from instrument to habitable ground.
Humans settle on the backs of mounts and glorify the One who subjected them; the ayah reverses the carrier perspective—humans become the load—and joins a back with spoken remembrance.
Hoarded metal brands foreheads, sides, and backs; stored goods become bodily punishment on the back, a concrete moral transformation of possessions into weight and pain.
What misers withhold will be made a collar around their necks on Resurrection Day; possessions turn into bodily restraint, bringing moral liability close to the section’s load-and-fetter meeting.
In the fasting ruling, God desires ease and not hardship; this gives a concrete legal setting for divine relief rather than leaving the section’s lightening as an abstract promise.
After purification rules, God says He does not desire to place hardship upon believers; the statement sets a boundary between divine command and a crushing burden.
Believers are told to strive while being reminded that God placed no constriction upon them in religion; duty remains, but it is not the back-breaking weight of the section.
The giver who fears God and affirms the best is “eased toward ease”; it generalizes the Prophet’s experienced lightening into a moral path open to others.
The deniers have shackles around their necks; this literalizes the restraint adjacent to the section’s dictionary cord and contrasts with a burden already removed.
Criminals are seen bound together in fetters; the image supplies an eschatological instance of the pranga-like restraint developed secondarily in the section.
The condemned are thrown into a narrow place bound together; confinement and binding show the bodily opposite of the section’s opening and unloading.
Shackles are put around the necks of the disbelievers as recompense for what they did; moral consequence becomes a physical restraint borne by the body.
Others are bound together in fetters under Solomon’s control; unlike punitive burdens borne at judgment, these bonds belong to a scene of constrained labor and rule.
With collars around their necks and chains, the deniers are dragged; the ayah closely supplies the hard restraint evoked by the section’s fetter cord.
Following 40:71’s collars and chains, this ayah makes the bound bodies be dragged into boiling water and fire; its own contribution is the forced movement imposed by the restraint.
The command “seize him and shackle him” makes fastening the guilty body an explicit spoken judgment, the inverse action to taking a burden off someone.
A seventy-cubit chain is threaded through the condemned person; after the seizure in 69:30, this ayah specifies the extraordinary binding instrument itself.
God warns of shackles and a blazing fire; the fetters show another possible weight laid upon bodies, set against the same surah’s “heavy word” entrusted to the Prophet.
Chains, collars, and a blaze are prepared for rejecters; the clustered restraint vocabulary directly develops the section’s secondary pranga image.
Whoever earns a fault and throws it onto an innocent person has “borne slander and manifest sin”; attempted transfer increases the accuser’s own burden rather than moving guilt away.
Those who harm innocent believers “bear slander and manifest sin”; the verb turns wrongful injury into a moral weight retained by the perpetrator.

Abel tells his brother that the attacker will return bearing the liability of both the intended murder and his own sin; this is accrued responsibility, not an innocent person volunteering to absorb another’s guilt.
The record is “set down” and criminals fear what it contains; the named placing verb moves from unloading a body to presenting the complete account of the deeds that make a moral burden.
God “sets down the just balances” for Resurrection, so no soul is wronged; placing here begins exact moral weighing rather than relieving a bearer.
At judgment the Book is set down and prophets and witnesses are brought; the same verb introduces disclosure and just decision, showing that not every وضع is release.
The earth brings out “its burdens”; a vast bearer discharges what was hidden inside it, giving a cosmic counterpart to a load leaving the human body.

A pregnancy begins as a light load and then grows heavy; the progression lets weight be known through the bearer’s changing bodily condition, as the section knows the unnamed load through the back’s strain.
Moses asks God to appoint a wazīr from his family; the shared w-z-r root has become a helper in responsibility, establishing a boundary between help with a mission and transfer of moral guilt.
Moses asks that his strength be reinforced through Aaron; this bodily language explains what the requested wazīr of 20:29 contributes without claiming that Aaron bears Moses’s personal vizr.
Moses asks that Aaron share in his task; shared work provides the positive counterpart to the impossible proposal that someone assume another person’s guilt.
God gives Moses the Book and makes his brother Aaron a wazīr with him; revelation’s heavy task has a companion-helper even though accountable burdens remain personal.
Moses asks that his more eloquent brother be sent as support who confirms him; the verse specifies speech and assistance as shareable burdens of mission.
God promises to strengthen Moses’s arm through his brother; bodily support supplies a concrete alternative to a back left creaking alone under a task.
The rhetorical reminder that God found the Prophet an orphan and sheltered him parallels the section’s retrospective question about a past vulnerability already relieved.
The reminder that God found the Prophet searching and guided him adds another concrete before-and-after act in the same direct divine address.
God found the Prophet in need and enriched him; relief from lack completes the preceding surah’s series of remembered divine interventions, analogous in stance to taking off the unnamed load.
People are carried on livestock and ships; the human body becomes cargo rather than bearer, a useful reversal of the section’s person under a load.
God carries human progeny in a laden ship; both vessel and passengers participate in bearing, widening the section’s carrier-load relation beyond a human back.
God promises to heal the breasts of believers through victory; the front of the body is made the felt site of relief, paralleling the section’s opened breast and relieved back.
Revelation is called healing for what is in the breasts; it links dhikr-like instruction with inward relief at the same bodily site named at the section’s front.
Moses says his breast constricts and his tongue does not move freely, then asks that Aaron be sent; mission-pressure, bodily constriction, speech, and assistance meet in one prophetic complaint.

Joseph orders his men to put the brothers’ merchandise inside their saddlebags; this plausibly recalls the section’s dictionary bundle filled with goods, though the ayah does not call the baggage a vizr or stress its weight.
The brothers open their baggage and find their merchandise returned; it continues 12:62’s packed-goods scene and illustrates the portable object behind the dictionary sense, but not bodily strain.

The drinking cup is placed in the brother’s saddlebag; object, container, and carriage closely match the mechanics of the section’s bundle definition, though the purpose is concealment rather than burden.
A camel-load is offered for recovery of the missing cup; this names a measured cargo as reward, a plausible literal comparator for vizr before its moral extension.
The oath by “those bearing a load” evokes carriers under weight, perhaps winds or clouds; the relation is concrete, but the bearers are not identified in the ayah and no relief occurs.

The heavens almost rupture, the earth splits, and mountains collapse; this may parallel the section’s weight becoming perceptible through a bearer’s physical failure, though 19:91 supplies a blasphemous claim rather than an actual carried object.
The cause of 19:90’s cosmic strain is the claim that the Merciful has taken a son; its own contribution is the intolerable utterance, making the parallel to a back-straining load indirect.
The heavens nearly split from above while angels glorify God; cosmic strain and raised praise meet suggestively with the section’s creaking weight and dhikr, but the ayah does not identify a burden.

Had the Qur’an descended on a mountain, it would have humbled and split from fear of God; alongside 73:5’s heavy word, this offers a possible image for revelation’s felt weight, while the section deliberately leaves its vizr unnamed.

God’s promised forgiveness of the Prophet’s earlier and later dhanb may meet the dictionary path from vizr to sin and divine removal, but the section itself refuses to identify its load as a particular fault.
The Prophet is commanded to seek forgiveness for his dhanb; this is relevant only to the section’s secondary “vizr as sin” sense and should not be used to name the unspecified burden.
The command to seek forgiveness for the Prophet’s dhanb and for believers may illuminate one possible moral sense of a removed vizr, but the lexical and contextual bridge remains indirect.

The Prophet may nearly consume himself in grief because people do not believe; this supplies a specific bodily strain that could belong among the unnamed pressures behind the image, though the section does not equate it with the vizr.
The Prophet may nearly destroy himself because the people are not believers; the intense mission-grief is a plausible component of back-breaking pressure, but no load vocabulary is used.
The Prophet is told not to let his soul depart in regrets over the misled; it names a burdening grief that divine address restrains, while leaving the link to the section’s load conjectural.
The Messenger is described as deeply distressed by the believers’ suffering and solicitous for them; this specific concern may help explain prophetic weight, but it cannot specify the unnamed vizr.
The ayah refers to fat “carried by their backs”; it shares back-and-carrying anatomy but describes tissue on animals, so it serves only as a lexical boundary around the section’s burden scene.

No female conceives or gives birth except with God’s knowledge; “puts down” retains the bodily delivery sense, but without an explicit load or hardship the correspondence is thinner than 46:15 and 65:4.
No female bears or gives birth without God’s knowledge; the carrying-and-delivery pair faintly parallels a burden put down, though its point is divine knowledge rather than relief.
